This algorithm then calculates the values for every 30 minutes for the next 60 minutes to provide another complete set of 300 minutes of data. The 30-minute plots are generated for every 60-minute period, and this process continues until the results are averaged. Both approaches reduce noise by averaging the data points, resulting in better statistical representation. It should be noted that these methods cannot be used to replicate a single trend, as there is still the potential for the anti-trend to be negative, or have generally greater exposure than the original trend. Data is only limited to short periods, ranging from a full day to two days for this purpose. Performance increases when the time window is increased to three days; however, accumulating all cities across the \(X\) axis when traveling through multiple cities increases the \(Y\) axis, yielding more uncertainty and less precision in the GPS tracking. The time-window method has the advantage that data is readily available across a large area when filtered through the Google Maps API. For the 24-hour data stream, we collected data for 24 hours from multiple cities over a 1 day period, and we have capped the \(X\) axis at 24 hours to prevent further inaccuracies. The cost improvement and data density is large enough that the price on this method is competitive. The 24-hour GPS tracker has an average cost of less than $120, per hour; with only 3 minutes of itemized expense per hour, this puts the cost from the 24-hour GPS tracker at $3600 per hour. 3. Methods
The multicell GPS tracking data collected by a mobile GPS unit serves as the primary source of mobile phone locations, phone activity, and lessons learned. To improve the accuracy of the tracking data and to make accurate corrections, we also resort to anonymized data that includes GPS values from users using either Nobel or Motorola smartphones as well as data derived from software events using the crash apps installed on these smartphones. In addition, Greg Andrade, the person in charge of the tracking data, explains that mobile phone activity data is mostly transmitted over Wi-Fi networks, and that Bluetooth and EDGE can account for about \(10\%\) of the total tracking data. While mobile phone location is tracked using dead reckoning, it is important to calculate the accuracy of the data.

As described above, reference governors compute a feasible virtual reference signal \(v_{t}\) at each time \(t\) that ensures constraint satisfaction. More specifically, the virtual reference \(v_{t}\) is chosen such that, if it were applied constantly to the system (3), then the constraints (2) would be satisfied for all future time steps. Such a virtual reference is computed using the maximal output admissible set (MAS) [24].

**Definition 1:** The maximal output admissible set \(\mathcal{O}_{\Delta}\) of a system \(\chi_{t+1} = A\chi_{t} + B_{w}\omega_{t}\), \(\omega_{t} \in \mathcal{W}\), subject to constraints \(y_{t} = C\chi_{t} + D_{w}\omega_{t} \in \mathcal{Y}\) is defined as

\[\mathcal{O}_{\Delta} := \left\{x \in \mathbb{R}^{n} :: \chi_{0} = x, \chi_{t+1} = A\chi_{t} + B_{w}\omega_{t}, C\chi_{t} + D_{n}\omega_{t} \in \mathcal{Y} \forall \omega_{t} \in \mathcal{W}, t \in \mathbb{N} \right\}\]

The MAS is the set of all initial conditions for which constraint satisfaction is guaranteed for any sequence of disturbances \(w_{t} \in \mathcal{W}\) and for all times. Furthermore, in order to ensure a sufficient rate of convergence, we employ a \(\lambda\)-contractive set in the proposed reference governor scheme.

**Definition 2:** For a system \(\chi_{t+1} = A\chi_{t} + B_{w}\omega_{t}\), \(\omega_{t} \in \mathcal{W}\), a set \(\mathcal{X} \in \mathbb{R}^{n}\) is \(\lambda\)-contractive with some \(\lambda \in (0, 1)\) if \(\mathcal{X}\) is convex, closed, \(0 \in \text{int} \,\mathcal{X}\), and \(A\mathcal{X} \oplus B_{w}\mathcal{W} \subseteq \lambda\mathcal{X}\).

Finally, recall that \(S_{K} = (I_{n} - A_{K})^{-1}B\) maps from a virtual reference \(v_{t}\) to the corresponding steady state of the undisturbed stabilized system. We define the error between the state \(x_{t}\) and the steady state corresponding to the reference \(v_{t}\) by

\[e_{t} := x_{t} - S_{K}v_{t}.\]

Next, consider a constant reference \(v_{t} \equiv v\). Then, the system dynamics (3) for an extended state written in error coordinates are given by

\[v_{t+1} = v_{t}\] (5a)

\[e_{t+1} = A_{K}e_{t} + B_{w}w_{t}\] (5b)

\[y_{t} = C_{L} + (C_{R} + D)v_{t} + D_{w}w_{t},\] (5c)

with \(v_{0} = v\) and \(e_{0} = x_{0} - S_{K}v\). Similar to [18, 23], we denote by \(\mathbb{O}_{\Delta}^{\kappa}\) the MAS of system (5) with (5b) replaced by

\[e_{t+1} = \frac{1}{\lambda} (A_{K}e_{t} + B_{w}w_{t})\] (6)

for some \(\rho(A_{K}) < \lambda < 1\) and with constraints \(y_{t} \in \mathcal{Y}\). We make use of this MAS \(\mathbb{O}_{\Delta}^{\kappa}\) in our OCO-RG scheme in Section III-C. Note that, since \(\mathcal{Y}\) is compact, convex, and \(0 \in \text{int} \,\mathcal{Y}\) by Assumption 2, the MAS \(\mathbb{O}_{\Delta}^{\kappa}\) is closed, convex, and \(0 \in \text{int} \,\mathbb{O}_{\Delta}^{\kappa}\) [24].

**B. Constraint tightening**

In this section, we develop a constraint tightening that ensures robustness of the proposed approach with respect to the disturbances \(w_{t}\) acting on system (3). Similar to robust model predictive control approaches in the literature [25], we rely on constraint tightening based on a robust positively invariant (RPI) set in order to ensure robust constraint satisfaction for the proposed OCO-RG scheme.

**Definition 3:** A set \(\mathcal{P}\) is called robust positively invariant for a system \(\chi_{t+1} = A\chi_{t} + B_{w}\omega_{t}\), \(\omega_{t} \in \mathcal{W}\), if \(A\mathcal{P} \oplus B_{w}\mathcal{W} \subseteq \mathcal{P}\) holds.

Let \(\mathcal{P}^{\lambda}\) be an RPI set for system (6). It can be shown that the minimal RPI set \(\mathcal{P}_{\Delta}^{\kappa}\) for system (6) is given by

\[\mathcal{P}_{\Delta}^{\kappa} := \bigoplus_{i=0}^{\infty}\left(\left(\frac{1}{\lambda}A_{K}\right)^{i}\frac{1}{\lambda}B_{w}\mathcal{W}\right) \subseteq \mathcal{P}^{\lambda},\] (7)

compare [24]. Let \(\bar{\mathcal{Y}}\) be a convex, compact subset of \(\mathcal{Y}\) such that \(0 \in \bar{\mathcal{Y}} \subseteq \text{int} \,\mathcal{Y}\). Then, we define the tightened set of admissible steady-state references by

\[\bar{\mathcal{S}}_{v} := \{v \in \mathbb{R}^{m} :: (C S_{K} + D) v \in \bar{\mathcal{Y}} \oplus D_{w} \mathcal{W} \oplus C \mathcal{P}^{\lambda}\}.\]

Note that \(\bar{\mathcal{S}}_{v}\) is convex, because \(\bar{\mathcal{Y}}\) is convex. In the following, we use the tightened set \(\bar{\mathcal{S}}_{v}\) within the OGD algorithm.

\[\bar{\mathcal{S}}_{v} := \{v \in \mathbb{R}^{m} :: (C S_{K} + D) v \in \bar{\mathcal{Y}} \oplus D_{w} \mathcal{W} \oplus C \mathcal{P}^{\lambda}\}.\]

Note that \(\bar{\mathcal{S}}_{v}\) is convex, because \(\bar{\mathcal{Y}}\) is convex. In the following, we use the tightened set \(\bar{\mathcal{S}}_{v}\) within the OGD algorithm.

**C. Robust OCO-RG scheme**

In this section, we introduce the proposed combination of OGD and the reference governor. The robust OCO-RG scheme is given in Algorithm 1. Compared to [18], the main differences are in the definitions of the MAS \(\mathbb{O}_{\Delta}^{\kappa}\) and the set \(\bar{\mathcal{S}}_{v}\), which were modified in order to take disturbances into account and ensure robust constraint satisfaction.

As described above, the cost functions \(L_{t}\) are time-varying and a priori unknown, i.e., at each time \(t \in \mathbb{N}\), we only have access to the previous cost functions \(L_{0}, \ldots, L_{t-1}\). Therefore, it is generally impossible to compute the minimizing input of (4) online. Instead, similar to, e.g., [7], [18], and the feedback optimization framework (compare Section I), Algorithm 1 aims to track the a priori unknown and time-varying optimal steady states \((\eta_{t}, \theta_{t})\) given by

\[\eta_{t} := \arg\min_{r \in \bar{\mathcal{S}}_{v}} L_{t}^{s}(r), \quad \theta_{t} := S_{K}\eta_{t}.\]

Moreover, at time \(t = 0\), no cost functions are known to Algorithm 1 and it simply applies an initial reference \(r_{0}\) in above algorithm. For \(t \geq 1\), the following updates determine a new set of optimal solutions as

\[\bar{\mathcal{S}}_{v}^{*} := \bigcup_{k=1}^{\infty}\left(\left(\frac{1}{\lambda}A_{K}\right)^{k}\frac{1}{\lambda}B_{w}\mathcal{W}\right) \subseteq \mathcal{S}_{v}^{k}\]

and

\[\bar{\mathcal{G}}_{v}^{k} := \bigcap_{r \in \bar{\mathcal{S}}_{v}}\left(\left(\frac{1}{\lambda}A_{K}\right)^{k}\left[\frac{1}{\lambda}B_{w}\mathcal{W} - \frac{R_{w}}{1+\lambda}\left(\frac{1}{\lambda}A_{K}\right)\right]^{k}\left[1+\frac{1}{\lambda}\frac{1}{\lambda}B_{w}\mathcal{W} - \frac{R_{w}}{1+\lambda}\left(\frac{1}{\lambda}A_{K}\right)\right]^{k}\right)
